passage: Freya was new at the school in Manchester, and when she told Alejandro she was from Chile he made a quick tsk sound with his tongue, and turned back to his lunch. Freya's face fell. In her town a tut like that could mean “no, I don't agree.” She said nothing. Then Alejandro added, still tutting softly, “Poor you, that's a long flight!” Freya blinked. In his family a tongue click meant “oh dear, I feel for you.” “Oh,” she said slowly. “I thought you were annoyed.” “No!” He laughed. “Sorry, that's how my grandmother sounds.”

qa.q: Where was Freya from?
qa.a: She was from Chile.

qa.q: Why did Freya's face fall when Alejandro tutted?
qa.a: In her town a tut like that could mean disapproval, so she took it as annoyance at her.

qa.q: What helped Freya and Alejandro sort out the mix-up?
qa.a: Freya said what she had thought and Alejandro explained his meaning, so they did not stay stuck on wrong guesses.

qa.q: How might Alejandro have felt on hearing that Freya thought he was annoyed?
qa.a: He may have felt surprised and a little embarrassed, since he had meant sympathy. 😅

grounding: A tut or tongue-click can mean disapproval in one place and sympathy in another, so a listener should not jump to conclusions.

passage: During the Class 5 morning assembly at a school in Pune, Deepak leaned over and whispered a wrong answer to the quiz question. Mahima, standing behind, gave a quick “tsk” and rolled her eyes to the ceiling. Deepak flushed. “She's annoyed with me,” he thought, and stared at his shoes. After assembly Mahima came up. “Sorry, I was tutting at myself. I forgot the answer too, and I felt silly.” In her family a tsk was for her own mistakes. Deepak let out a breath. “I thought it was for me,” he said, and they walked to class together.

qa.q: Where did the quiz happen?
qa.a: At the Class 5 morning assembly at a school in Pune.

qa.q: What did Deepak think Mahima's tsk meant, and what was it actually?
qa.a: He thought she was annoyed with him, but she was tutting at herself for forgetting the answer and feeling silly.

qa.q: What could Deepak try next time he is unsure about a sound like that?
qa.a: He could ask, “Was that about me?” before staying upset, because the same tut can carry different meanings.

qa.q: How might Mahima have seen Deepak's flushed face?
qa.a: She may have noticed he was embarrassed and realised her tsk could be misread, so she explained it.

grounding: A tongue-click can be disapproval, self-annoyance or something else, and a child checks before concluding.

passage: I'm Harsha, and on Saturday I went to Ojas's house. When Ojas told his grandmother he'd scraped his knee at football, she clicked her tongue three times: “Tch, tch, tch.” I thought she was cross with him, the way my coach tuts when we mess up. But Ojas didn't look worried. He just held out his knee. His grandmother shook her head slowly, face soft, and dabbed it with a cloth. “Tch, tch. Poor boy.” Later Ojas told me that in his house that sound means “oh, you poor thing.” I don't know what his grandmother was thinking, but it didn't sound like my coach's tut at all.

qa.q: What had Ojas scraped at football?
qa.a: Ojas had scraped his knee.

qa.q: What was Ojas's grandmother most likely feeling when she clicked her tongue?
qa.a: She most likely felt sympathy and concern for Ojas, as her soft face and “Poor boy” show, not disapproval.

qa.q: What could Harsha do next time a tongue-click seems cross?
qa.a: Harsha could look at the face and tone, or ask, before deciding it means disapproval.

qa.q: How did Ojas understand the sound?
qa.a: Ojas knew that in his house the sound means “oh, you poor thing,” so he wasn't worried at all.

grounding: Shows a tongue-click meaning disapproval in one setting and sympathy in another, and why a listener should not jump to conclusions.

passage: Monday: In their first week in Istanbul, Mohit asked the corner shopkeeper if he had mango juice. The man tilted his head back, raised his eyebrows and made a short “tsk.” Mohit's face went hot. He's annoyed with me. He left without buying anything. Wednesday: At school, his classmate Emre explained. “That's just ‘no’ here. Head back, tsk. It's not rude.” Mohit told his sister Bhavna. She laughed. “The bus driver did that to me! I thought he hated me.” Friday: Mohit went back and asked for orange juice. The shopkeeper nodded and smiled. When Mohit asked for a straw, he got a “tsk.” This time Mohit just smiled back.

qa.q: What did Mohit ask for on Monday?
qa.a: Mohit asked if the shopkeeper had mango juice.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling when the shopkeeper made the “tsk”?
qa.a: Mohit felt embarrassed and hurt, thinking the shopkeeper was annoyed with him.

qa.q: What helped Mohit understand the sound?
qa.a: His classmate Emre explained that head back with a tsk simply means no there, so Mohit could stop taking it personally.

qa.q: What did Bhavna's story about the bus driver show?
qa.a: It showed she had made the same mistake, reading a plain no as dislike.

grounding: Shows a child learning that a tongue-click can mean a plain no in another culture, not disapproval.

passage: Saurabh, you just went “ch-ch” when your friend dropped his ice cream. So did I at your age, and it got me into trouble. Let your Parul Dadi tell you. We had just moved to Leicester, and I was nine. In the playground a girl fell and cut her lip. I ran over saying, “Ch, ch, ch,” the way my mother always did when someone was hurt. The dinner lady grabbed my arm. “Don't you tut at her! That's rude!” I didn't have the English to explain. I just cried. The next day my mother came in and told the teacher it was our sound for sympathy. After that the dinner lady would say, “Ah, your ch-ch,” and smile.

qa.q: Where had young Parul's family just moved?
qa.a: They had just moved to Leicester.

qa.q: What was young Parul feeling when the dinner lady scolded her?
qa.a: She felt shocked and upset, and helpless because she didn't have the English to explain her sympathy.

qa.q: What choice did Parul's mother make, and why did it help?
qa.a: She went in the next day and explained the sound meant sympathy, which cleared up the misunderstanding for good.

qa.q: How did the dinner lady first read Parul's “ch, ch”?
qa.a: The dinner lady heard it as a rude tut of disapproval, not knowing it was a sound of sympathy in Parul's family.

grounding: Shows a tongue-click meaning sympathy in one culture and disapproval in another, and a listener jumping to the wrong conclusion.

passage:
The bus crawled through the Hyderabad traffic jam, packed so tight Kamal could barely lift an arm. When it lurched, his fare coins flew out of his hand and rolled under a dozen feet.

"Tch, tch, tch," went Sarika Aunty, his mother's friend, squeezed in beside him. Kamal's face burned. She thinks I'm careless.

Then Sarika Aunty bent down, knees creaking, and fished coins out from between sandals. "Tch, poor boy, in this crush anyone would drop them."

Kamal stared. The same sound. A minute later he asked the conductor if the bus went to the zoo. The conductor clicked his tongue once and tossed his head back. No. Same sound, different meanings, Kamal thought, and none of them what he'd feared.

qa.q: Where did Kamal's coins roll?
qa.a: Under a dozen feet.

qa.q: What did Kamal feel when he first heard Sarika Aunty's "Tch, tch, tch"?
qa.a: Embarrassed, as his burning face shows, because he took the sound as disapproval, as if she thought him careless.

qa.q: What should Kamal do the next time he hears a tut or a click?
qa.a: Wait for the tone, words and actions that follow, since the same sound can mean sympathy, a no, or disapproval.

qa.q: What did Sarika Aunty's clicking actually mean?
qa.a: Sympathy: she felt sorry for him in the crush and bent down to help pick up the coins.

grounding: It shows a child reading a tongue-click as disapproval, then finding the same sound can carry sympathy or a no depending on tone and context.
